stops.name: Mumbai
stops.title: Salt air and the first rain
stops.dek: The monsoon arrived the same afternoon we did, and the city didn't slow down for either of us.
stops.quote: Mumbai in July is loud, soaked and completely unbothered.

story.text: We landed into a sky the colour of wet slate. Four of us, one shared umbrella that broke before we left the airport, and a plan that mostly consisted of eating. By the time the cab reached Marine Drive the first proper downpour had begun and the promenade emptied in about forty seconds, except for the chai sellers, who simply moved their stoves under the nearest awning and kept pouring.

We dumped the bags at a guesthouse in Colaba and walked straight back out. Leopold Cafe was loud and full of steam. The Gateway of India was half hidden behind spray from the harbour wall, and every few minutes a wave would clear the railing and soak whoever was taking a selfie. Nobody minded. That is the thing about Mumbai in July: everyone is already wet, so nobody is in a hurry to stay dry.
Dinner was at a tiny Irani place near Kala Ghoda, bun maska and keema pav, then a long walk along the Queen's Necklace with the lights coming on in a curve all the way to Malabar Hill.

story.title: The train, the doors, the vada pav

story.text: The next morning we rode the local from Churchgate with the doors open, the way everyone does, holding the overhead bar and leaning out just enough to feel the rain. The trick is to stand on the side away from the platform, otherwise you get swept off at Dadar by a wall of office workers.
Mumbai in July is loud, soaked and completely unbothered.

Outside Dadar station we ate vada pav standing up, dripping chutney onto our shoes. Then Bandra for the afternoon: graffiti lanes in Ranwar, a long sit on the rocks at Bandstand watching the sea throw itself at the sea link, and far too much coffee.
Buy a first-class day pass on the local. It costs a little more, the carriages are calmer, and you can hop on and off all day.
We ended at Juhu, where the beach was almost empty and the bhel puri stall was not. It was the right place to start.

stops.name: Lonavala
stops.title: Clouds you can walk through
stops.dek: Two hours up the expressway, the ghats swallowed the road and gave us back waterfalls.
stops.quote: The fog tore open for ten seconds and the whole valley was there.

story.title: Up the ghats into the cloud

story.text: Somewhere past Khopoli the expressway climbs into the cloud and stays there. One minute you can see the trucks ahead, the next you are driving through milk. Lonavala in the monsoon is less a town than a weather system. Every ridge is streaming, every hairpin has a waterfall, and every waterfall has a family standing under it in their clothes.

We checked into a hillside homestay run by an uncle who refused to let us leave without a second breakfast. Poha, then pakoras, then chai, then advice. The advice was mostly about which waterfalls were safe and which ones were for showing off. We nodded and then went to the showing-off ones anyway.

Bhushi Dam is basically a giant staircase with a river running down it. You sit on the steps and the water pours over your legs. It is cold, slippery, absolutely packed and one of the most joyful places I have ever been. Someone's speaker was playing old Bollywood songs and half the dam was singing along.

story.title: Tiger's Leap and the ten-second view

story.text: We walked out to Tiger's Leap at seven and saw absolutely nothing for twenty minutes. Just white. Then the fog tore open for maybe ten seconds and the whole valley was there, impossibly green, a river at the bottom, before it closed again. We stood there for another half hour hoping it would happen twice. It did not.
The fog tore open for ten seconds and the whole valley was there.

The afternoon was Karla Caves, two thousand years old, cut straight into the cliff. The big chaitya hall has a wooden ceiling that is somehow still there, and the inside is so quiet after the noise of the road that we all started whispering without meaning to.
On the way back we stopped for bhutta roasted on coals with lime and chilli rubbed on it, and bought far too much chikki. Maganlal is the famous one. Every shop claims to be the original.
Go to the viewpoints at sunrise on a weekday. By ten the road to Tiger's Leap is a parking lot.

stops.name: Pune
stops.title: Old wadas, new coffee
stops.dek: A city of Peshwa gateways and third-wave cafes, separated by about one auto ride.
stops.quote: The lanes are narrow enough that the rain only reaches you in stripes.

story.text: Pune felt like exhaling. After two days of waterfalls we wanted something with a roof. We spent the first morning around Shaniwar Wada and the old peths, where the lanes are narrow enough that the rain only reaches you in stripes, and every second doorway has a carved wooden frame older than our grandparents.

Shaniwar Wada is mostly walls and gates now. The palace inside burned down in 1828, but the Delhi Gate with its elephant spikes is still there, and the gardens are a good place to sit and listen to a guide tell the ghost story with great enthusiasm.

Tulshibaug market sells everything: brass lamps, plastic buckets, wedding garlands, a very small and very angry parrot. We bought a set of steel tumblers we did not need and carried them for the rest of the trip.
The lanes are narrow enough that the rain only reaches you in stripes.

The real reason to come, though, is breakfast. Misal pav with a fiery tarri, eaten at a steel table while the cook argues cricket with the regulars. We went back twice. The second time he gave us extra farsan without asking, which we took as acceptance.

In the afternoon we drove up to Sinhagad fort. The road is all switchbacks and the top was in cloud, but the stalls at the summit sell kanda bhaji and thick curd in clay pots, and that is reason enough. The evening was Koregaon Park, very serious coffee and a long argument about whether Pune or Mumbai has the better food. Pune won, narrowly.
Do the peths on foot with a local walking tour. They know which courtyards you are allowed to step into.

stops.name: Mahabaleshwar
stops.title: Strawberries in the mist
stops.dek: The plateau was quieter than we expected, and greener than anywhere we've been.
stops.quote: We had Arthur's Seat to ourselves and the sound of water everywhere.

story.title: The plateau in the off season

story.text: Monsoon is off-season up here, which means half the viewpoints are hidden in cloud and none of the crowds turn up. The drive in through Wai and Pasarni ghat is the kind of road where you stop every ten minutes because the view is ridiculous, then stop again because the view is gone and there is a waterfall instead.

We stayed in an old colonial bungalow with a fireplace, a dog called Biscuit and a caretaker who made hot chocolate at nine every night whether you asked or not. It rained for fourteen hours straight. Nobody complained.

We had Arthur's Seat to ourselves, a cold wind coming up off the Savitri valley and the sound of water everywhere. Venna Lake had exactly one boat out, rowed by a very determined couple in raincoats. We hired the second one and got lost in fog about thirty metres from the jetty.
We had Arthur's Seat to ourselves and the sound of water everywhere.

story.title: Jam, cream and the Pratapgad road

story.text: Strawberry season is long gone by July, but the farm sheds still sell jam and thick strawberry cream, and we were not about to say no. Mapro garden was open and bright pink. We bought jars for every relative and ate one of them in the car.

The drive down to Pratapgad the next morning was the most beautiful road of the whole trip. The fort itself sits on a ridge with clouds moving through the walls, and there are about five hundred steps, each one wet. At the top a man sold us roasted peanuts in paper cones and told us the whole Shivaji and Afzal Khan story with sound effects.
Carry a proper rain jacket, not an umbrella. The wind on the viewpoints turns umbrellas inside out in seconds.

stops.name: Alibaug
stops.title: Ending at the edge of the sea
stops.dek: Down from the ghats to the Konkan coast, and a ferry back to where it all began.
stops.quote: The rain held off long enough for an actual sunset.

story.text: After a week in the hills the sea felt enormous. The road down from the plateau drops through Mahad and then flattens into rice fields so green they look fake, with egrets standing in every single one like they were placed there by a set designer.

We stayed in a cottage near Kihim with a coconut grove for a garden and a hammock that four grown men are not supposed to sit in at once. We found that out. The owner's mother cooked lunch every day and refused to tell us what was in the sol kadhi.

In the afternoon we walked out to Kolaba Fort at low tide, ankle-deep across the sand bar, timing the walk back so the sea did not cut us off. Inside there is a temple, a freshwater well and a lot of crabs who did not want visitors.
The rain held off long enough for an actual sunset.

story.title: Last light and the ferry home

story.text: The fish thali at a little place on the main road ruined every other fish thali for us. Surmai fry, prawn curry, rice bhakri and the pink sol kadhi again. We ordered a second round and then lay in the hammock for two hours, carefully this time.

On the last evening the rain held off long enough for an actual sunset at Kihim, the first one of the whole trip. The next morning we took the ferry from Mandwa back across the harbour to the Gateway, the city we had started in, slightly drier this time and about three kilos heavier each.
Take the Mandwa ferry instead of the road from Mumbai. It is an hour on the water instead of three in traffic.
